title: Merge sort and insertion sort
footer: 2.1 Lesson 9: Merge sort and insertion sort
starter: Deal yourself seven playing cards. Sort them into order and write down exactly what you did. Which algorithm was it closest to?
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Merge sort: splitting
facts: Split the list in half, then split each half, and keep going.
Stop when every piece holds a single item, which is sorted by definition.
This is the divide part of divide and conquer.
stations.challenge: Show how 8, 3, 5, 1 is split down to single items.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Split the list in half, then split each half, and keep going.
Also credit: Stop when every piece holds a single item, which is sorted by definition.

questions.q: Put these stages of the splitting phase in order for the list 8, 3, 5, 1.
Why does splitting stop at single items?
questions.a: A list of one item is already in order

stations.name: Merge sort: merging
facts: Take two sorted pieces and combine them into one sorted piece.
Compare the first item of each, take the smaller, and repeat.
Keep merging pairs until one sorted list remains.
stations.challenge: Merge 3, 8 with 1, 5 and show each comparison.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Take two sorted pieces and combine them into one sorted piece.
Also credit: Compare the first item of each, take the smaller, and repeat.

questions.q: Put the merging of 3, 8 with 1, 5 into order.
questions.a: Compare 3 and 1, take 1 → Compare 3 and 5, take 3 → Compare 8 and 5, take 5 → Only 8 remains, so take 8

questions.q: When merging two sorted lists, which item is taken next?
questions.a: The smaller of the two items at the front

stations.name: Merge sort: the whole thing
facts: Split all the way down, then merge all the way back up.
It is much faster than a bubble sort on large lists.
It needs extra memory to hold the pieces, so it does not sort in place.
stations.challenge: Describe merge sort in two sentences: one for splitting, one for merging.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Split all the way down, then merge all the way back up.
Also credit: It is much faster than a bubble sort on large lists.

questions.q: What is the main disadvantage of a merge sort?
questions.a: It needs extra memory to hold the pieces while merging

questions.q: Why is merge sort much faster than bubble sort on large lists?
questions.a: The work grows far more slowly as the list gets longer

stations.name: Insertion sort
facts: Treat the first item as a sorted section of one.
Take the next item and move it left until it is in the right place within that section.
Repeat until every item has been inserted.
stations.challenge: Run an insertion sort on 4, 2, 7, 1 and show each step.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Treat the first item as a sorted section of one.
Also credit: Take the next item and move it left until it is in the right place within that section.

questions.q: Sort this list with an insertion sort. Tap two items to swap them.
Where does an insertion sort put each new item?
questions.a: Into its correct position within the sorted section on the left

stations.name: Comparing the three sorts
facts: Bubble: simplest, slowest, sorts in place.
Insertion: simple, faster than bubble, sorts in place, very fast on nearly sorted data.
Merge: most complex, much faster on large lists, needs extra memory.
stations.challenge: Make a table comparing the three sorts on speed, memory and complexity.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Bubble: simplest, slowest, sorts in place.
Also credit: Insertion: simple, faster than bubble, sorts in place, very fast on nearly sorted data.

questions.q: Which sorting algorithm does each statement describe?
questions.a: Compares neighbouring items and swaps them = Bubble sort; Splits the list until single items remain = Merge sort; Builds a sorted section one item at a time = Insertion sort; Needs extra memory to hold the pieces = Merge sort; The slowest of the three on a large list = Bubble sort; Like sorting cards in your hand = Insertion sort

questions.q: Which sort would you choose for a million records with plenty of memory?

stations.name: Answering sorting questions
facts: Name the algorithm and describe its distinctive action: swap neighbours, insert into a sorted section, or split and merge.
If asked to show the steps, show the list after each pass or insertion.
Comparisons usually mean 'when does it stop' and 'how much memory'.
stations.challenge: Plan a six-mark answer comparing bubble sort and merge sort.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Name the algorithm and describe its distinctive action: swap neighbours, insert into a sorted section, or split and merge.
Also credit: If asked to show the steps, show the list after each pass or insertion.

questions.q: Sort this list with an insertion sort.
Which is the strongest comparison sentence?
questions.a: A merge sort is much faster on large lists, but a bubble sort sorts in place and needs no extra memory

final.name: Final challenge: sort it out

questions.q: Sort this list with an insertion sort.

questions.a: Repeats passes until no swaps are made = Bubble sort; Divides the problem, then combines the answers = Merge sort; Moves each new item back into the sorted part = Insertion sort; The only one of the three that is not in place = Merge sort; Very fast when the list is almost in order = Insertion sort; The easiest of the three to program = Bubble sort

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Describe how an insertion sort works.
points: Name the algorithm and describe its distinctive action: swap neighbours, insert into a sorted section, or split and merge.
If asked to show the steps, show the list after each pass or insertion.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

exam.q: Show the stages of a merge sort on the list 6, 2, 9, 4.
points: Split all the way down, then merge all the way back up.
Name the algorithm and describe its distinctive action: swap neighbours, insert into a sorted section, or split and merge.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

exam.q: Compare a bubble sort with a merge sort, giving one advantage of each.
points: Compare the first item of each, take the smaller, and repeat.
It is much faster than a bubble sort on large lists.
Split the list in half, then split each half, and keep going.
Split all the way down, then merge all the way back up.
It needs extra memory to hold the pieces, so it does not sort in place.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
